newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian MP warns of civil war over race.
newsitem.headline: Australian MP warns of civil war over race.

text.p: A parliamentarian at the centre of a heated Australian debate over immigration and aboriginal welfare policies warned on Sunday of civil war in Australia if migrants and Aborigines continued to get special treatment.

"When you look at what is going on in Ireland, Bosnia, Rwanda -- civil wars because of different races, different cultures -- that's what I don't want to see in this country," independent Member of Parliament Pauline Hanson said.
"Everyone should be treated the same. We have got to get together as one, otherwise we are going to end up like those other countries," she told Sydney's The Sun-Herald newspaper.
Hanson, who said in her maiden speech to parliament last month that Australia was in danger of being "swamped by Asians", said she wanted all immigration to cease, at least temporarily.

She also linked immigration to high unemployment levels and high crime rates in some areas, singling out the Sydney suburb of Cabramatta, which is populated largely by Asian, mainly Vietnamese, migrants.
"You can't turn your back on the problem that is happening out there -- it is happening and people know it," she said.
She denied however she was a racist.
"I am not a racist, I know in my heart I am not a racist," she said. But she said she believed multiculturalism, both for migrants and Aborigines, had gone too far.

Hanson, a fish-and-chip shop owner from conservative Queensland state, was elected as an independent in March after being dumped by Prime Minister John Howard's Liberal Party over her controversial stand on immigration, multiculturalism and what she sees as excessive aboriginal welfare programmes.

Howard has been criticised for not making a stronger stand against Hanson, who, polls show, enjoys wide community support, although he has spoken out broadly against intolerance and non-discriminatory immigration.
An opinion poll published in last Tuesday's Sydney Morning Herald newspaper found 48 percent of respondents backed Hanson, while only 38 percent disagreed.
Her controversial views have also been criticised for jeopardising Australia's relationship with its Asian neighbours.
Australia admits about 100,000 migrants a year, about a third from Asia.
